extracted.intended_audience: legislators, statesmen, merchants, and readers of political economy
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for judging when to restrict or liberalize foreign trade, impose duties, or grant monopolies (including defense exceptions and transitional considerations). Aimed at guiding legislators and policymakers on commercial regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private interest promotes public good (market coordination)
rubrics_metrics.description: By pursuing his own interest, he frequently promotes that of the society more effectually than when he really intends to promote it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discourage affectation of trading for the public good; private agents often allocate capital more effectively than statesmen. Avoid laws that attempt to direct private people in how to employ their capitals; such direction assumes authority dangerous in any single person, council, or senate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local knowledge superior for capital allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the species of domestic industry which his capital can employ, and of which the produce is likely to be of the greatest value, every individual, it is evident, can in his local situation judge much better than any statesman or lawgiver can do for him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators should not attempt to determine individuals' uses of capital; doing so is unnecessary and hazardous. Examples: tailor vs shoemaker, shoemaker vs tailor, farmer employing different artificers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly of the home market usually useless or hurtful
rubrics_metrics.description: To give the monopoly of the home market to the produce of domestic industry, in any particular art or manufacture, ... must in almost all cases be either a useless or a hurtful regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If domestic produce can be as cheap as foreign, the regulation is useless; if it cannot, it is generally hurtful because it directs industry away from more valuable employment and diminishes the exchangeable value of annual produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization and mutual exchange (household prudence analog)
rubrics_metrics.description: All of them find it for their interest to employ their whole industry in a way in which they have some advantage over their neighbours, and to purchase with a part of its produce ... whatever else they have occasion for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What is prudence in private families scales to nations: buy foreign goods that are cheaper to obtain, and employ domestic capital where it has advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infant-industry/protectionist argument is weak for total national wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: By means of such regulations, indeed, a particular manufacture may sometimes be acquired sooner than it could have been otherwise, and after a certain time may be made at home as cheap, or cheaper, than in the foreign country. But ... the sum-total, either of its industry, or of its revenue, can ever be augmented by any such regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although protection can hasten a manufacture's domestic development, immediate effect of regulation is to diminish revenue; capital only augments by saving out of revenue, so protection does not reliably raise total industry or revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not struggle with overwhelming natural or acquired advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural advantages which one country has over another, in producing particular commodities, are sometimes so great, that it is acknowledged by all the world to be in vain to struggle with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: raising grapes in Scotland via glass/hot-beds would cost many times more than importing wine; it is absurd to divert vastly more capital and industry to such efforts. Whether advantage is natural or acquired is irrelevant: buy where cheaper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection tends to benefit merchants and manufacturers more than farmers
rubrics_metrics.description: Merchants and manufacturers are the people who derive the greatest advantage from this monopoly of the home market. ... It is in the fetching and carrying manufactures, accordingly, that foreign trade is chiefly employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufactures (especially finer ones) are easily transported and easily undersold by foreigners; protection thus often advantages merchants and manufacturers rather than graziers or farmers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider transport costs, perishability, and bulk when assessing import effects
rubrics_metrics.description: If the importation of foreign cattle ... were made ever so free, so few could be imported, that the grazing trade of Great Britain could be little affected. ... Salt provisions are not only a very bulky commodity, but when compared with fresh meat they are a commodity both of worse quality...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bulky, perishable, or high-transport-cost goods (live cattle, salt provisions, corn) are less likely to disrupt domestic producers because transportation limits imports; empirical evidence (small numbers imported) supports this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equalize duties when domestic produce is taxed
rubrics_metrics.description: When some tax is imposed at home upon the produce of the latter, it seems reasonable that an equal tax should be imposed upon the like produce of the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imposing an equal duty on imports of the same taxed produce prevents taxation from unfairly diverting domestic demand; in practice governments often lay heavier duties to assuage complaints from domestic producers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad compensatory duties for general taxes are impractical and harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: This general enhancement of the price of labour is a case which differs ... First, It might always be known with great exactness, how far the price of such a commodity could be enhanced by such a tax; but how far the general enhancement of the price of labour might affect that of every different commodity ... could never be known with any tolerable exactness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two objections: (1) impossible to proportion duties accurately across many commodities; (2) taxes on necessaries mimic poor soil/climate by raising subsistence costs, therefore it's absurd to add duties that compound the burden and hinder natural employment adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retaliation only justified when likely to secure repeal
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be good policy in retaliations of this kind, when there is a probability that they will procure the repeal of the high duties or prohibitions complained of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If retaliation is unlikely to procure repeal, it generally harms many classes of one's own country while benefiting only some; historical examples given (French/Dutch/English mutual restrictions) show retaliation can escalate into war or long mutual harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retaliatory protection often imposes a tax on the whole country
rubrics_metrics.description: This may ... give encouragement to some particular class of workmen among ourselves, and, by excluding some of their rivals, may enable them to raise their price in the home market. Those workmen however, who suffered by our neighbours prohibition, will not be benefited by ours. On the contrary, they, and almost all the other classes of our citizens, will thereby be obliged to pay dearer than before for certain goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation retaliating against foreign prohibitions tends to channel benefits to a narrow group while spreading costs widely; treat such measures as real taxes on the nation rather than true compensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore free importation gradually when many people's livelihoods depend on protected industries
rubrics_metrics.description: Humanity may in this case require that the freedom of trade should be restored only by slow gradations, and with a good deal of reserve and circumspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gradual removal may be humane when protection has created many jobs. However, Smith cautions that the disorder from sudden removal is often exaggerated: many protected manufactures export goods competitively and would retain home markets; displaced workers often find other employment, and capital remains in-country to reemploy labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense-related exceptions (navigation acts) justify trade burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: The first is, when some particular sort of industry is necessary for the defence of the country. ... The act of navigation, therefore, very properly endeavours to give the sailors and shipping of Great Britain the monopoly of the trade of their own country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an industry is critical to national defense (e.g., sailors and shipping), restrictions, prohibitions, or heavy burdens on foreign competitors may be wise. Smith lists specific navigation act provisions (ownership/crewing rules, exclusions, double duties) and notes national security trumps mere opulence concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workers' mobility and collateral industries mitigate harm of liberalization
rubrics_metrics.description: By the reduction of the army and navy ... more than 100,000 soldiers and seamen ... were all at once thrown out of their ordinary employment: but though they no doubt suffered some inconveniency, they were not thereby deprived of all employment and subsistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: discharged soldiers/seamen largely absorbed into merchant service or other occupations; manufacturers are generally better placed to switch trades than soldiers. Capital and collateral similar manufactures remain to employ labor, so unemployment and wage collapse from liberalization likely less severe than feared.
